To tell apart the verbs expressing doubt or denial: démentir, nier, prétendre.

To recognise fake news and respond to a rumour.
Monday, 2 September 2029. An online paper has published an article claiming the La Duchère hall will not be ready. A journalist calls Radu, who now runs the building site together with Ioana.
Mr Popescu? Pierre Duval, from the paper “Lyon Matin”. According to an article published this morning, the La Duchère hall would not be ready for the start of the school year. Do you confirm?
No, I deny it completely. The work is almost finished. I don’t know where this information comes from.
According to the article, the roof was allegedly badly built, and the ceiling window supposedly lets the rain in.
I admit there was a small waterproofing problem in July. But it was repaired in two days. I want to make clear that the hall passed all the safety inspections.
The article also claims the budget was exceeded by thirty per cent.
That’s false. We exceeded the budget by two per cent, because of the price of wood. The overrun was accepted by the region in June. Everything is written in the minutes.
Who, in your opinion, would be behind this article?
I don’t want to accuse anyone. But I stress that the author contacted neither the town hall, nor the Conservatoire, nor our firm before publishing.
Can you give me a date for the inauguration?
Yes. It will take place on Friday 20 September, at five p.m. The mayor confirmed his attendance this morning. And I’ll add that you are invited.
(laughs) Thank you. May I quote you?
Of course. But quote me correctly, please. Two per cent, not thirty.
Promise. One last question: is it true that the hall will bear Hélène Morel’s name?
That I can neither confirm nor deny. The name will be announced by the mayor on the day of the inauguration. Come, and you’ll find out.
had (“il y a eu” = there was)
I want to (“tenir à” = to be keen to)
“Suh-reh”: the conditional of “être”. Don’t confuse it with “sera” (future) = “suh-ra”.
In the press and in formal speech, “dire” is replaced by more precise verbs that show the ATTITUDE of the speaker:
L’article affirme que le budget a été dépassé.
Le maire a déclaré que la salle était prête.
Il a précisé que c’était deux pour cent.
Il a ajouté que le journaliste était invité.
Il a souligné que l’auteur n’avait contacté personne.
Il a reconnu qu’il y avait eu un problème.
Sequence of tenses (ch. 38) applies: if the reporting verb is in the past, the tenses shift: “Il a précisé que les travaux SERAIENT finis en septembre.”
Le chef de projet a démenti la rumeur.
Il nie avoir dépassé le budget.
L’article prétend que le toit est mal construit.
False friend: “prétendre” does NOT mean “to pretend” (= faire semblant), but “to claim, to maintain”. It shows the journalist doesn’t necessarily believe the claim.
To indicate where a piece of information comes from:
In your opinion, who would be behind the article?
From a reliable source, the name will be Hélène’s.
“Selon moi” = in my opinion (rarer than “à mon avis”). “D’après moi” is also possible.
The French press uses the CONDITIONAL for information it has not verified. The present for a current situation, the past for a past fact:
La salle ne serait pas prête.
Le toit aurait été mal construit.
La fenêtre laisserait passer la pluie.
The hall is reportedly not ready.
English uses “reportedly”, “allegedly”, “is said to” for the same idea. The difference: in French the conditional is almost COMPULSORY in serious press when information is not confirmed.

According to an article published this morning, the hall would not be ready.

It had all started on a Monday morning, 2 September, at a quarter past seven. Radu was still in the bathroom when his phone vibrated on the kitchen table. Then it vibrated again, and again. When he finally came out, a towel around his neck, he found eleven messages and four missed calls.

The first message was from Chloé: “Have you seen this??” There was a link. Radu clicked, and the headline appeared in big black letters: “La Duchère: the music hall, a one-million fiasco?” Below it, a photo of the site, taken on a rainy day, with a blue tarpaulin on the roof.

He read the article standing up, without even sitting down. According to the author, the hall would never be ready for the start of the school year. The roof had allegedly been badly built, the big ceiling window supposedly let the rain in, and the budget had reportedly been exceeded by thirty per cent. “According to a source close to the site,” he wrote, “the children would spend the winter in an unheated gym.”

The last paragraph was the worst. The author claimed the project had been entrusted to “an inexperienced Romanian intern, the brother-in-law of the firm’s boss”. Radu reread the sentence three times. His hands were shaking. It wasn’t completely false, and that was exactly what hurt.

At eight he was at the office. Ioana was already there, with Nathalie, in front of the screen. Nobody spoke. Rose-Hélène, whom Julien hadn’t taken to the crèche yet, was sitting on the floor stacking pencils. She looked up and cried happily: “Rara!” She was the only happy person in the room.

“Who wrote this?” Radu asked. Nathalie shrugged. The site was called “Lyon Vérité”. There was no address, no phone number, only a name, “Marc D.”, and an email address. “It’s not a real newspaper,” Nathalie said. “But look: the article has already been shared two thousand times.”

Ioana read the comments in a low voice. Some were kind, most were terrible. “More money thrown out of the window.” “They’d have done better to fix the roads.” “The children of La Duchère don’t need violins, they need jobs.” She shut the computer with a snap.

“Right,” she said. “We’re not going to cry. We’re going to answer. But we’ll answer with facts, not with anger.” She took a sheet of paper and started a list. The roof problem: true, but fixed. The budget: false, two per cent, not thirty. The intern: Radu hadn’t been an intern since June, he had been hired.

“And the brother-in-law?” Radu asked in a small voice. Ioana looked at him for a long time. “You’re my brother, not my brother-in-law. And you weren’t chosen because you’re my brother. You were chosen because you designed the best hall. The region’s jury voted without knowing your name. That’s a fact too.”

At ten the office phone rang. It was a journalist from “Lyon Matin”, a real paper, the one Odile read every morning. His name was Pierre Duval. Nathalie handed the receiver to Radu. “It’s your project,” she said. “It’s up to you to speak.” Radu took a deep breath and answered.

He would never remember exactly what he said. He would only remember that he spoke slowly, as Ioana had advised him. He denied what was false. He admitted what was true. He gave the exact figures. And at the end, almost without thinking, he invited the journalist to the inauguration.

When he hung up, Nathalie clapped softly. “You were perfect,” she said. “Well, almost. You said ‘I deny it completely’ four times.” Radu laughed for the first time that day. Rose-Hélène, who understood nothing, clapped too.

In the afternoon, Julien came to pick up his daughter looking odd. He had spent the morning at La Duchère, preparing the new term with the teachers. “The children have seen the article,” he said. “The parents too. Inès didn’t want to take out her clarinet. She asked if the instruments were going to be taken back.”

That sentence hurt Radu more than the whole article. He could bear people speaking badly of him. But he couldn’t bear a twelve-year-old girl being afraid of losing Lucien Roux’s clarinet. He grabbed his jacket. “Where are you going?” Ioana asked. “To La Duchère. I’m going to show them the hall. Now.”

At five, about twenty children and as many parents were waiting in front of the site gate. Julien had sent everyone a message. Mrs Mansouri was there, arms crossed as always. Mr Mansouri, who had just woken up after his night shift, still had red eyes. Mrs Roux had come by taxi, with her walking stick.

Radu opened the door, and they went in. The hall wasn’t quite finished. The chairs, the curtains and the paint on one wall were missing. But the light fell from the big ceiling window, exactly as Yanis had drawn it a year earlier on a sheet from his exercise book. The parquet smelled of new wood.

The children stopped in the middle of the room and looked up. Nobody said anything. Then Yanis whispered: “That’s my window.” He said it so softly that only those closest heard him. His mother uncrossed her arms.

“Mr Architect,” asked a father Radu didn’t know, “the article says the roof lets the rain in. Is it true?” Radu looked up at the ceiling. “It rained all Thursday night,” he replied. “Look at the floor. Do you see a single drop?” The parents looked at the parquet, then at the ceiling, then at the parquet again.

“I admit that in July there was a problem,” Radu went on. “A company had fitted a seal badly. Water got in during a storm. I won’t lie to you: I was very scared. But the seal was replaced in two days, and since then the hall has passed every inspection. I’ll show you the papers, if you like.”

Nobody wanted to see the papers. Inès went up to Mrs Roux and took her hand. “Madame,” she asked, “are they going to take my clarinet back?” The old lady smiled. “My dear, that clarinet is yours. Lucien decided it, from up there. And nobody, do you hear me, nobody argues with Lucien.”

Inès opened her case, right there, in the middle of the empty hall. She played the first notes of the waltz. The sound bounced off the bare walls, louder than in any concert hall. Yanis went to fetch his cello from his father’s car. A boy took a flute out of his schoolbag. Within ten minutes, half the orchestra was playing.

Mrs Mansouri took out her phone and filmed. That same evening the video was online, with a single sentence: “Here is the hall that lets the rain in.” It was shared more than ten thousand times in one night. Five times more than the article.

The next day, “Lyon Matin” published Pierre Duval’s article. The headline was simple: “The false alarm”. The journalist had done his job. He had checked the region’s minutes, called the town hall, spoken to a mother. He had quoted Radu correctly: two per cent, not thirty. And the “Lyon Vérité” site took its article down that evening, without a word of apology.

One question remained: who was Marc D.? It was Chloé who had found the answer, one Friday evening, searching online. Marc D. was called Marc Delorme. He was the nephew of the boss of a building company that had lost the tender for the hall the year before.

“Do we file a complaint?” Chloé asked, her eyes shining. Nathalie thought for a long time. Then she shook her head. “No. A lawsuit would last two years, and everyone would still be talking about that article. I’d rather people talked about the hall. The best answer to fake news is a real inauguration.”

That evening Radu called Lucia, who was spending the end of the summer in Seville with her grandparents. He told her everything: the article, the comments, Inès’s fear, the video, the ten thousand shares. She listened without interrupting. Then she handed the phone to her grandfather.

Don Manuel spoke a strange French, learned in Paris cabarets in the sixties. “Radu,” he said, “when I was young, a journalist wrote that I played the guitar like a donkey. I kept that article for fifty years. Do you know why?” Radu didn’t. “Because the next day a thousand people came to hear me, to see the donkey.”

Radu laughed so loudly that the neighbour downstairs knocked on the ceiling. Then Lucia took the phone back, and her voice turned serious. “There’s something else,” she said. “My grandmother wants to come to the wedding. In May. In Lyon. She has never flown.” Radu smiled. He already knew a grandmother who was afraid of planes, and who had crossed Europe by coach.

In the following days the office received dozens of messages. A pensioner from Villeurbanne offered to donate his piano. A school in Vénissieux asked if its pupils could visit the hall. And a letter, a real letter with a stamp, arrived from Paris. It was signed Isabelle Bernard.

“My mother sent me the Lyon Matin article,” Isabelle wrote. “She cut it out and stuck it on a sheet, with a note: ‘Your father would have been proud of this boy.’ I don’t know if my mother is right. But I know my father hated two things: lies and people who give up. You didn’t give up. I’ll come on the 20th.”

That evening Radu dropped by Odile’s, on rue d’Austerlitz. She was waiting for him on the landing, with the Lyon Matin article folded in four in her apron pocket. “Henri always said a lie goes round the harbour while the truth is putting its shoes on,” she said. “But the truth always gets there in the end. It just walks more slowly, that’s all.”

She served him a herbal tea and biscuits that were too dry, and Victor, the old cat, fell asleep on his lap. Radu didn’t dare move for an hour. Before he left, Odile whistled a few bars of the waltz, very softly, as every morning. “To bring you luck,” she explained. “On the 20th I’ll be in the front row. And I’ll whistle louder than the violins.”

There was one last rumour left, and that one nobody wanted to deny. In the neighbourhood people said the hall would bear Hélène’s name. The children were sure of it. Mrs Roux pretended to know nothing. Julien smiled whenever he was asked. And the mayor, questioned by Pierre Duval, replied that he could neither confirm nor deny it.

On Thursday 19 September, the eve of the inauguration, Radu stayed alone in the hall until midnight. The chairs had arrived, the curtains too. The wall was painted. On the façade, a plaque was hidden under a white sheet. He knew what was written underneath, but he had promised to say nothing, not even to Ioana.

Before leaving, he went out in front of the hall. The little lime tree, the one from the Parc de la Tête d’Or, had lost a few leaves. They were already yellow. Radu picked one up and put it in his wallet, next to Lucia’s photo. Then he looked up at the big roof window, where the moon was reflected.

“Well, Madame Hélène,” he said aloud, to no one. “According to our information, tomorrow will be a beautiful day.” He waited, as if he hoped for an answer. There was only the wind in the lime tree. But for the first time in two weeks, Radu slept the whole night, without looking at his phone even once.
